title: Lateral Dermoid Cyst: The Classic Pediatric Orbital Choristoma
summary: Lateral dermoid cysts are the most common pediatric orbital tumors, representing benign choristomatous sequestrations of ectoderm at the zygomaticofrontal suture. While slow-growing, they require surgical excision with an intact capsule to prevent severe granulomatous inflammation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A dermoid cyst is a choristoma—normal histological tissue located in an abnormal anatomical site. In ophthalmology, the lateral dermoid is the most frequent subtype, typically occurring at the zygomaticofrontal suture. These cysts are lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium and contain dermal appendages like hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

rows: Not easily palpable; may be firm

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Painless, slow-growing mass at the lateral brow.
Smooth, rubbery, or firm consistency on palpation.
Non-pulsatile and non-reducible (unlike cephaloceles).
Usually mobile under skin but fixed to underlying periosteum.
Minimal effect on visual acuity unless large enough to induce astigmatism.
Rarely causes motility restriction or diplopia.

sections.title: Imaging Findings (CT/MRI/USG)
content: CT: Well-circumscribed, round/oval mass with fat-density center (-30 to -100 HU).
CT Bone Windows: Focal thinning or 'scalloping' of the zygomatic bone.
MRI T1: High intensity (hyperintense) signal due to lipid content.
MRI T2: Variable signal; often hypointense compared to T1.
B-Scan USG: Well-demarcated with low internal reflectivity and internal echoes (keratin).

rows: Similar but lacks dermal appendages (no hair/sebum).
Older adults, slower growth, posterior location.
Translucent cyst of lacrimal ductule, fluctuating size.
Plexiform 'bag of worms' feel, associated with NF1.

sections.title: Red Flags & Emergency Signs
content: Sudden Onset Pain/Erythema: Indicates cyst rupture and granulomatous reaction.
Dumbbell Configuration: Posterior extension through the zygomatic bone into the temporal fossa.
Rapid Increase in Size: Raises suspicion for malignancy or acute hemorrhage.
Significant Proptosis or Optic Nerve Compression: Rare in superficial cysts.
Bony Destruction: Rather than simple scalloping, suggests aggressive lesions.

sections.title: Histopathology: Textbook Findings
content: Cyst wall: Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium.
Lumen content: Desquamated keratin, sebum, and sometimes hair shafts.
Dermal Appendages: Sebaceous glands, sweat glands, and hair follicles in the wall.
If ruptured: Intense chronic granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Foreign body reaction to keratin).

content.explanation: Suture (usually Zygomaticofrontal), Smooth (regular borders), Scalloping (bone remodeling on CT).

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Incision choice - Lateral brow (within hair) or lid crease (better scar cosmesis).
Step 2: Blunt dissection through orbicularis muscle and septum to reach the cyst capsule.
Step 3: Careful dissection around the cyst, maintaining an intact capsule to prevent rupture.
Step 4: Separation from the periosteum at the suture line (often the most adherent point).
Step 5: Removal of the cyst and inspection for bone defects (dumbbell extension).
Step 6: Irrigation of the cavity and meticulous closure of layers.

rows: Risk of recurrence and chronic fistula.
Rare; occurs in medial dermoids or deep orbital extensions.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out 'dumbbell' extension with imaging if the cyst is not clearly superficial.
A 'tail' extending toward the bone suture is a classic intraoperative finding.
If a dermoid ruptures during surgery, wash the area thoroughly with saline to prevent 'lipogranulomatous' inflammation.
In children, surgery is often deferred until 6-12 months of age unless growth is rapid.
Unlike a mucocele, a dermoid cyst is NOT connected to the paranasal sinuses.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: The prognosis for lateral dermoid cysts is excellent following complete surgical excision. Recurrence is extremely rare if the capsule remains intact. Long-term follow-up is primarily for cosmetic monitoring and to ensure no late-onset inflammatory response occurs if a micro-rupture happened during surgery.
